source: Initial economy model for the dashboard (FRI design note, 13 November 2026; wage layer added 18 November 2026)

scenarios.preamble:
We define three scenarios for different levels of AI development:

- Slow progress
- Moderate progress
- Rapid progress

In the following scenarios, we consider the development of AI capabilities, not adoption. Regulation, social norms, or extended integration processes could all prevent the application of AI to all tasks of which it is capable.

Reasonable people may disagree with our characterization of what constitutes slow, moderate, or rapid AI progress. Or they may expect to see slow progress observed with some AI capabilities and moderate or fast progress in others. Nevertheless, we ask you to select which scenario, in sum, you feel best represents your views.

We consider a capability to have been achieved if there exists an AI system that can do it:

* Inexpensively: with a computational cost not exceeding the salary of an appropriate 2025 human professional using the same amount of time to attempt the task.
* Reliably: what this means is context-dependent, but typically we mean as reliably as, or more reliably than, a human or humans who do the same tasks professionally.

The scenarios refer to capability at the end of 2030.
scenarios.footnote: Level 5 autonomy is defined as, “can operate the vehicle on-road anywhere within its region of the world and under all road conditions in which a conventional vehicle can be reasonably operated by a typically skilled human driver. This means, for example, that there are no design-based weather, time-of-day, or geographical restrictions on where and when the ADS can operate the vehicle. However, there may be conditions not manageable by a driver in which the ADS would also be unable to complete a given trip (e.g., white-out snow storm, flooded roads, glare ice, etc.) until or unless the adverse conditions clear.”

indicators.name: Summary
indicators.text: By the end of 2030 in this slower-progress future, AI is a capable assisting technology for humans; it can automate basic research tasks, generate mediocre creative content, assist in vacation planning, and conduct relatively standard tasks that are currently (2025) performed by humans in homes and factories.

indicators.name: Research
indicators.text: Researchers can benefit from literature reviews on almost any topic, written at the level of a capable PhD student, yet AI systems rarely produce novel and feasible solutions to difficult problems. As a result, genuine scientific breakthroughs remain almost entirely the result of human-run labs and grant cycles. Nevertheless, AI tools can support other research tasks (e.g., copy editing and data cleaning and analysis), freeing up time for researchers to focus on higher-impact tasks.

indicators.name: Problem-solving
indicators.text: AI can handle roughly half of all freelance software-engineering jobs that would take an experienced human approximately 8 hours to complete in 2025, and if a company augments its customer service team with AI, it can expect the model to be able to resolve most complaints.

indicators.name: Creativity
indicators.text: Writers enjoy a small productivity boost; models can turn out respectable short stories, but full-length novels still need heavy human rewriting to avoid plot holes or stylistic drift. AI can make a 3-minute song that humans would blindly judge to be of equal quality to a song released by a current (2025) major record label.

indicators.name: Agency
indicators.text: At home, an AI system can draft emails, top up your online grocery cart, or collate news articles, and—so long as the task would take a human an hour or less and is well-scoped—it performs on par with a competent human assistant. With a few prompts, AI can create an itinerary and make bookings for a weeklong family vacation that feels curated by a discerning travel agent.

indicators.name: Robotics
indicators.text: Self-driving car capabilities have advanced, but none have achieved true level-5 autonomy. Meanwhile, household robots can make a cup of coffee and unload and load a dishwasher in some modern homes—but they can’t do it as fast as most humans and they require a consistent environment and occasional human guidance. In advanced factories, autonomous systems can perform specific, repetitive tasks that require precision but little adaptability (e.g., wafer handling in semiconductor fabrication facilities).

indicators.name: Summary
indicators.text: By the end of 2030, in this middle-of-the-road future, AI is capable of being an effective collaborator across creative, corporate, and technical arenas.

indicators.name: Research
indicators.text: R\&D teams can lean on autonomous lab systems with human research assistants to make rapid advances in solar-cell chemistries or fusion-reactor components, although the inventions are improvements rather than revolutions.

indicators.name: Problem-solving
indicators.text: Almost all freelance software-engineering jobs requiring 5 days or fewer of effort from experienced humans can be tackled by AI, and if a company wants to replace nearly all of its human customer service team with AI, it can probably get away with it, provided customers are not opposed in principle to AI customer service.

indicators.name: Creativity
indicators.text: AI can draft 100-thousand-word novels solid enough for current (2025) mainstream publishers to release with typical levels of editing by a human publisher and can create a 5-minute song that humans would blindly judge to have breakout potential, exceptional emotional depth, and be of equal quality to the best songs released by current (2025) record labels.

indicators.name: Agency
indicators.text: An AI agent can not only craft a well-curated weeklong vacation itinerary, but it can also make last-minute adjustments to bookings in response to unexpected weather, travel delays, or individual requests. Boardrooms are still run by people, but executive teams can delegate multiday operational projects to agentic software that reliably juggles vendors, budgets, and contingencies.

indicators.name: Robotics
indicators.text: Level-5 robo-taxis that can go anywhere a human driver can go finally exist, as do robots that can navigate any home in the US, make a cup of coffee and unload and load a dishwasher as fast and reliably as most humans and without any human guidance. Robots in advanced factories can adapt to different tasks without extensive reprogramming or equipment changes, making real-time decisions, and have increased physical mobility.

indicators.name: Summary
indicators.text: By the end of 2030, in the rapid-progress world, AI systems are capable of competing with the best human minds and workers, and can surpass them. Human creativity and leadership remain valued, but mostly for setting high-level vision—day-to-day execution can be left to silicon-based systems.

indicators.name: Research
indicators.text: Autonomous researchers can collapse years-long research timelines into days, weeks, or months, creating game-changing technologies, such as materials that revolutionize energy storage, or bespoke cancer cures.

indicators.name: Problem-solving
indicators.text: No human freelance software engineer can outperform AI. The same goes for customer service (e.g., call center and support chat), paralegal, and administrative workers (e.g., bookkeepers or scheduling assistants).

indicators.name: Creativity
indicators.text: Models have become so capable that AI can create an album of the same caliber as the Grammy Album of the Year. Additionally, a single AI agent can generate a Pulitzer- (or Booker Prize-) caliber novel according to current (2025) standards, adapt the book into an engaging two-hour movie,

indicators.name: Agency
indicators.text: negotiate the resulting book and movie contracts, and launch the marketing campaigns for both while its sibling agents manage the book publishing company and movie studio at the level of highly competent CEOs.

indicators.name: Robotics
indicators.text: Not only do Level-5 robo-taxis exist, but they are, on average, 99.9% safer than human-piloted cars and can venture anywhere off-road that a competent human driver can. Meanwhile, robots can navigate an arbitrary home anywhere in the world, make a cup of the most popular local hot beverage, clean and put away the dishes according to the local custom, fix any plumbing issues that arise while they’re doing the dishes--and they can do it all faster and more reliably than most humans and without human guidance. Robots in advanced factories can autonomously perform the full range of tasks requiring the highest levels of dexterity, coordination, and adaptive decision-making.

industries.name: Real estate and rental and leasing

occupations.name: Arts, design, entertainment, sports and media

components.name: Real value added
components.text: Real value added of {industry} in {year}: the industry's output net of the inputs it buys, with price changes removed, as an index with the 2025 annual value = 1 (1.10 means 10% above 2025).
components.source: BEA, GDP by Industry: chain-type quantity index for value added, annual, rebased to 2025 = 1

components.name: Price of value added
components.text: Price of value added of {industry} in {year}: the industry's dollar value added divided by its real value added, as an index with 2025 = 1.
components.source: BEA, GDP by Industry: chain-type price index for value added, annual, rebased to 2025 = 1

components.name: Labor productivity
components.text: Labor productivity of {industry} in {year}: real value added per hour actually worked, as an index with 2025 = 1.
components.source: Real value added (BEA) divided by hours actually worked in the industry (CPS microdata, government employees assigned to government)

components.name: Hours per employed person
components.text: Hours actually worked per employed person per year in {industry} in {year} (CPS; every government employee counted in federal or state and local government).
components.source: CPS microdata: annual hours actually worked divided by employment, by industry

components.name: Capital input
components.text: Capital input of {industry} in {year}: the flow of services from its buildings, equipment, software and data centers, valued at rental cost, as an index with 2025 = 1.
components.source: BEA-BLS Integrated Industry-Level Production Account: capital input by industry

components.name: Labor share
components.text: Labor share of {industry} in {year}: compensation of employees as a share of the industry's nominal value added, from 0 to 1.
components.source: BEA, GDP by Industry: compensation of employees divided by value added

components.name: Occupation mix
components.text: Share of the employed people in {industry} whose job is in {occupation} in {year}, from 0 to 1 (the 22 shares of an industry are rescaled to sum to 1).
components.source: CPS public-use microdata, tabulated by FRI with a fixed rule (government employees assigned to government)

components.name: Unemployment rate by occupation
components.text: Unemployment rate in {year} among people whose last job was in {occupation}: unemployed divided by employed plus unemployed, from 0 to 1.
components.source: CPS annual averages, table 25: unemployed persons by occupation

components.name: Unemployed with no occupation
components.text: Unemployed people in {year} not counted in any of the 22 occupation groups (almost all with no previous work experience), as a share of the labor force, from 0 to 1.
components.source: CPS: total unemployed minus the 22 occupation rows of table 25, divided by the labor force

components.name: Population 16 and over
components.text: Civilian noninstitutional population aged 16 and over in {year}, annual average, in millions.
components.source: CPS civilian noninstitutional population (FRED: CNP16OV)

components.name: Median weekly earnings by occupation
components.text: Median weekly earnings of full-time wage and salary workers in {occupation} in {year}, annual average, in current dollars.
components.source: CPS annual table 39: median weekly earnings of full-time wage and salary workers by occupation

components.name: 10th percentile of weekly earnings
components.text: 10th percentile of usual weekly earnings of all full-time wage and salary workers in {year}, the mean of the four quarters, in current dollars.
components.source: BLS Usual Weekly Earnings release, table 5

components.name: Median weekly earnings
components.text: Median usual weekly earnings of all full-time wage and salary workers in {year}, the mean of the four quarters, in current dollars.
components.source: BLS Usual Weekly Earnings release, table 5

components.name: 90th percentile of weekly earnings
components.text: 90th percentile of usual weekly earnings of all full-time wage and salary workers in {year}, the mean of the four quarters, in current dollars.
components.source: BLS Usual Weekly Earnings release, table 5

components.name: Employment Cost Index, wages and salaries
components.text: Employment Cost Index for wages and salaries (the pay of a fixed mix of jobs) in {year}, the mean of the four quarters, as an index with 2025 = 1.
components.source: BLS Employment Cost Index, wages and salaries (FRED: CIU1020000000000I)

components.name: Consumer prices (PCE price index)
components.text: Price index for personal consumption expenditures (the prices households pay) in {year}, annual average, as an index with 2025 = 1.
components.source: BEA PCE price index (FRED: PCEPI)

components.name: Work done with AI help
components.text: Share of the work of {occupation} in {year} done by a human with AI help, from 0 to 1.
components.source: No official source

components.name: Work done by machines alone
components.text: Share of the work of {occupation} in {year} done by a machine alone, with human oversight, from 0 to 1.
components.source: No official source

components.name: Human time with AI help
components.text: Human time needed in {year} for work of {occupation} done with AI help, relative to a human doing the same work alone (0.6 means 40% less time).
components.source: No official source

components.name: Oversight time for machine work
components.text: Human oversight time needed in {year} when a machine does work of {occupation} alone, relative to a human doing the same work alone.
components.source: No official source

components.name: Real GDP growth (direct)
components.text: US real GDP growth in {year}, annual average over annual average, in percent. For 2035, 2040 and 2050: the average annual growth rate since the previous year asked (2030, 2035, 2040).
components.source: BEA national accounts, real GDP (FRED: GDPCA)

components.name: Unemployment rate (direct)
components.text: US unemployment rate in {year}, annual average, in percent.
components.source: CPS annual average (FRED: UNRATE)

components.name: Labor force participation rate (direct)
components.text: US labor force participation rate in {year}, annual average, in percent.
components.source: CPS annual average (FRED: CIVPART)

components.name: Labor productivity growth (direct)
components.text: Growth of US labor productivity (real GDP per hour actually worked, whole economy) in {year}, in percent. For 2035, 2040 and 2050: the average annual growth rate since the previous year asked.
components.source: BEA real GDP divided by CPS total hours (FRI calculation)

components.name: TFP growth (direct)
components.text: US total factor productivity growth in {year} (output growth minus the share-weighted growth of capital input and hours, whole economy), in percent. For 2035, 2040 and 2050: the average annual growth rate since the previous year asked.
components.source: BEA-BLS integrated account, aggregated by FRI's formula

baselines.name: Nominal value added, 2025
baselines.text: Nominal value added of {industry} in 2025, in billions of current dollars.

baselines.name: Hours worked, 2025
baselines.text: Total hours actually worked in {industry} in 2025 (CPS, civilians, government employees in government), in millions of hours.

baselines.name: Employment, 2025
baselines.text: Employed persons in {industry} in 2025, annual average (CPS, government employees in government), in millions.

baselines.name: Labor share, 2025
baselines.text: Labor share of {industry} in 2025: compensation of employees divided by nominal value added, from 0 to 1.

baselines.name: Occupation mix, 2025
baselines.text: Share of the employed people in {industry} whose job is in {occupation} in 2025, from 0 to 1.

baselines.name: Unemployment rate by occupation, 2025
baselines.text: Unemployment rate in 2025 among people whose last job was in {occupation}, from 0 to 1.

baselines.name: Unemployed with no occupation, 2025
baselines.text: Unemployed people in 2025 not counted in any of the 22 occupation groups, as a share of the labor force, from 0 to 1.

baselines.name: Population 16 and over, 2025
baselines.text: Civilian noninstitutional population aged 16 and over in 2025, annual average, in millions.

baselines.name: Median weekly earnings by occupation, 2025
baselines.text: Median weekly earnings of full-time wage and salary workers in {occupation} in 2025, in dollars.

baselines.name: 10th percentile of weekly earnings, 2025
baselines.text: 10th percentile of usual weekly earnings of full-time wage and salary workers in 2025, mean of the four quarters, in dollars.

baselines.name: Median weekly earnings, 2025
baselines.text: Median usual weekly earnings of full-time wage and salary workers in 2025, mean of the four quarters, in dollars.

baselines.name: 90th percentile of weekly earnings, 2025
baselines.text: 90th percentile of usual weekly earnings of full-time wage and salary workers in 2025, mean of the four quarters, in dollars.

baselines.name: Employment Cost Index, 2025
baselines.text: Employment Cost Index for wages and salaries in 2025, mean of the four quarters, relative to the 2025 annual value (1 by definition, unless you expect revisions).

baselines.name: Consumer prices, 2025
baselines.text: PCE price index in 2025, annual average, relative to the 2025 annual value (1 by definition, unless you expect revisions).

baselines.name: Work done with AI help, 2025
baselines.text: Share of the work of {occupation} in 2025 done by a human with AI help, from 0 to 1.

baselines.name: Work done by machines alone, 2025
baselines.text: Share of the work of {occupation} in 2025 done by a machine alone, with human oversight, from 0 to 1.

baselines.name: Human time with AI help, 2025
baselines.text: Human time needed in 2025 for work of {occupation} done with AI help, relative to a human doing it alone.

baselines.name: Oversight time for machine work, 2025
baselines.text: Human oversight time needed in 2025 when a machine does work of {occupation} alone, relative to a human doing it alone.
